draft.title: The Children's Court
card: In NSW, the Children's Court hears most criminal charges against young people under 18. It is a separate court from the courts that hear adult cases.
It is a closed court. The public cannot sit in the courtroom, and only people involved in the case, such as the young person, their family and the lawyers, are usually there.

Its focus is rehabilitation, which means helping the young person change their behaviour and stay out of trouble. Punishment is not the only aim, and the court looks at the young person's needs and circumstances.

The names of young people are usually kept private. News media generally cannot publish a name that identifies a child involved in the case. This protects the young person's chances of starting again.
draft.remember: A closed court that aims to rehabilitate, and that usually keeps a young person's name private.

a.q: Which feature of the Children's Court best shows its focus on rehabilitation?
opts: It looks at the young person's needs and circumstances
It is open to the public so the community can watch
It hears cases from both young people and adults
It aims to deter others by publishing their name
a.why: Rehabilitation means helping the young person change, so the court considers their needs and circumstances. Open hearings and published names work against its aims, and it does not hear adult cases.
a.clue: Rehabilitation is about helping a young person change.

b.q: A 16-year-old in Newcastle is charged with stealing from a shop. A reporter wants to publish the teenager's name in the local paper. What is the usual position if the case is heard in the Children's Court?
opts: The name cannot usually be published
The name must be published to warn the public
The name can be published once the teenager turns 18
The name can be published if the family agrees
b.why: Names of young people in the Children's Court are usually kept private, so media generally cannot identify the teenager. The aim is to protect the young person's chance to move on, not to warn the public.
b.clue: Think about what the court tries to protect for a young person.

a.best: It looks at the young person's needs and circumstances

b.best: The name cannot usually be published

problems.detail: The card says only people involved in the case are usually in the courtroom. In NSW, media representatives are generally allowed to attend Children's Court criminal hearings (Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 s10), even though the general public is excluded. They just cannot publish identifying details.
The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('usually'), which echoes 'usual position' in the question stem. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: The Children's Court
card: In NSW, the Children's Court hears most criminal charges against young people under 18. It is a separate court from the courts that hear adult cases.
It is a closed court. The general public cannot sit in the courtroom during criminal hearings, though reporters are generally allowed to attend.

Its focus is rehabilitation, which means helping the young person change their behaviour and stay out of trouble. Punishment is not the only aim, and the court looks at the young person's needs and circumstances.

The names of young people are usually kept private. Even when reporters attend, they generally cannot publish a name or details that identify a child in the case. This protects the young person's chance to start again.
proposal.remember: A closed court that aims to rehabilitate, and that usually keeps a young person's name private.

a.q: Which feature of the Children's Court best shows its focus on rehabilitation?
opts: It looks at the young person's needs and circumstances
It is open to the public so the community can watch
It hears cases from both young people and adults
It aims to deter others by publishing their name
a.why: Rehabilitation means helping the young person change, so the court considers their needs and circumstances. Open hearings and published names work against its aims, and it does not hear adult cases.
a.clue: Rehabilitation is about helping a young person change.

b.q: A 16-year-old in Newcastle is charged with stealing from a shop. The case is heard in the Children's Court. What is a local reporter generally allowed to do?
opts: Attend the hearing but not publish the name
Attend the hearing and publish the name
Neither attend the hearing nor publish the name
Publish the name but not attend the hearing
b.why: The public is excluded, but reporters are generally allowed to attend. Being in the courtroom does not give them the right to identify the teenager, so the name stays private. Thinking a closed court shuts out reporters too is the common mistake.
b.clue: Being allowed in the room and being allowed to publish are separate rules.

b.best: Attend the hearing but not publish the name
